newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - TI sees chip market volatility.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - TI sees chip market volatility.

text.p: Texas Instruments Inc expects the key market for memory chips to show volatility in the short-term, with manufacturers' supply oustripping demand, Chief Financial Officer Bill Aylesworth said.

A recent recovery in prices for DRAM (dynamic random access memory) chips was due to a reduction of customers' inventories and expectations of strong personal computer sales, but prices could fall again, he said.
"We think the DRAM market is likely to remain volatile," Aylesworth told Reuters in a telephone interview.

"The indications all year have been supply generally in excess of demand, except for short periods of time like the last few weeks, and so we think it is likely that kind of condition will continue in the near-term," he said.
Memory chip inventories soared late last year and this, combined with growing inventories among customers, drove DRAM prices down about 80 percent.

That has battered TI's bottom line. The Dallas-based company today reported third quarter earnings, excluding charges, fell to $44 million, or $0.23 per share, from $289 million, or $1.48 a share, in the same period last year.
Aylesworth said the problem now is that manufacturers' inventories, which are difficult to track, have not yet been brought under control.

"We think we've completed the inventory depletion in our customers' shops, but there is a lot of capacity out there and that is where the supply is coming from," he said. "I think it is more likely to be volatile than it is to be stable in the near-term."
At the start of 1996, TI predicted the world semiconductor market would grow 20 percent this year. Aylesworth now says it will show a decline of about 10 percent.
Aylesworth said growth would return in 1997 but would be "moderate" and would not reach the 15-20 percent average shown by the industry in recent years. He made no specific projection.
"Moderate means below the trend level," he said.

In a bid to cut costs, TI plans to offer 5,300 U.S.-based employees early retirement. Aylewsorth said the plan, effective through year-end, would bring a fourth-quarter charge but that it was not clear how big it would be.
He did not say how many of the 5,300 eligible employees TI expects -- or hopes -- will take up the offer. The company has about 30,000 employees in the United States.
In another cost-cutting measure, TI said it will cut its capital spending program "significantly" in 1997. The company spent $2.3 billion this year to finance new R&D facilities in Dallas.
Aylesworth declined to say what capital spending would be in 1997 but said the reduction would help boost TI's finances.

"It'll be significant enough to have a favorable impact on our cash flow in 1997," Aylesworth said. "At the same time, it is consistent with our plan to fully support our growth areas in digital signal processing and mixed-signal manufacturing. We are not going to constrain that support."

Revenues from digital signal processors (DSPs) -- semiconductor chips that translate human speech, sound waves and other data into a computer-readable format -- were up more than 30 percent in the third quarter.
The DSP business made up about 40 percent of semiconductor revenues, while the share accounted for by DRAM chips has slipped to about 25 percent from almost 40 percent last year.
